body.statement: For the two-vertex equality-face construction, tying both missing outcomes strictly below the controls yields \(P_\delta(a)=1\), while maximizing over strict weak-order chambers only yields \(8/9\).
body.justification: This smallest reduction instance proves that equality faces are inferentially active.
body.gap: Tie-aware fixed-data tests retain average ranks, but no prior supplied-design completion result proves a strict loss from deleting equality strata.
body.consumer: It is a mandatory unit test for chamber enumeration and for the reduction converse.
body.proof_tex:
Here \(v=s=2\), \(e=1\), \(h=2\), \(B=2\), \(A_\star=6\), and
\[
W_\star=1+2\cdot6+2\cdot2+1=18.
\]
Tie the two missing vertex outcomes at a common value strictly below zero.  They form the lowest block, each with midrank \(3/2\).  Both guards pass, both vertex rows pass, and the unique edge row passes.  Including the actual row, the unnormalized upper-tail weight is
\[
1+2\cdot6+2\cdot2+1=18,
\]
so this completion has tail one.  No tail can exceed the total design mass one, and therefore the robust p-value is \(1\).

Now restrict attention to full-dimensional strict chambers for the two missing coordinates, so neither missing value is tied to the other or to an observed block.  If a guard fails, the actual row, at most one remaining guard, both vertex rows, and the edge row have total unnormalized weight at most
\[
1+6+2\cdot2+1=12.
\]
If both guards pass, both missing values are strictly below zero and, being distinct, have ranks \(1\) and \(2\).  The vertex-row threshold is \(r_i\le3/2\), so exactly one vertex row passes and contributes \(2\).  Their rank sum is \(3\), so the edge row also passes and contributes \(1\).  The two guards contribute \(12\), and the actual row contributes \(1\).  Hence every such all-guard strict chamber has tail
\[
\frac{1+12+2+1}{18}=\frac{16}{18}=\frac89.
\]
This is larger than the bound when a guard fails and is attained by either strict ordering below zero.  Therefore deletion of equality faces lowers the maximum from \(1\) to \(8/9\).
